name: Common House Gecko
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. A welcome resident that eats mosquitoes and other insects.
description: The common house gecko is the most widespread and familiar gecko in Southeast Asia, found on the walls and ceilings of virtually every home, shop, and restaurant after dark. A supreme coloniser, it has spread across the tropics aboard cargo ships and now inhabits every continent except Antarctica. Its distinctive chirping call — 'chak chak chak' — is a defining sound of tropical nights across the region.
funFact: The common house gecko produces a distinctive chirping call used for communication — in many Southeast Asian cultures, counting the number of calls is considered an omen for good or bad luck.

name: Tokay Gecko
dangerNotes: Will bite hard and hold on if handled. Bite is painful but not dangerous. Can draw blood. Do not handle.
description: The tokay gecko is the largest gecko in Southeast Asia and one of the most recognisable, with a stocky blue-grey body covered in vivid orange-red spots. Its loud, distinctive two-syllable call — 'to-KAY, to-KAY' — booms through tropical nights and is responsible for its common name. A powerful predator of insects, small lizards, and even young rodents, it is highly territorial and will bite aggressively if disturbed.
funFact: The tokay gecko's bite force is extraordinary relative to its size — it can bite hard enough to draw blood and will clamp down and refuse to release, earning it a fearsome reputation among locals.

name: Asian Water Monitor
dangerNotes: Can bite and whip with its powerful tail — both are painful and the bite carries bacteria. Large adults are formidable. Do not corner or approach.
description: The Asian water monitor is the second heaviest lizard on Earth and one of the most adaptable reptiles in Southeast Asia, thriving in everything from pristine mangroves to city drains and rubbish dumps. A powerful swimmer, it hunts fish, crabs, carrion, eggs, and small mammals. Revered in some cultures and feared in others, it is an essential scavenger in both natural and urban ecosystems throughout the region.
funFact: The Asian water monitor is one of the few lizards known to actively scavenge human waste in cities — Bangkok's Lumphini Park is famous for its population of large individuals that treat park visitors with total indifference.

name: Green Crested Lizard
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The green crested lizard is a slender, long-tailed agamid with vivid emerald-green colouring and a distinctive serrated crest along neck and back. An arboreal species, it perches motionless on branches and tree trunks where its colouring provides near-perfect camouflage. When stressed it can turn brown or dark — the basis of the widespread but false belief that it is a chameleon. A swift, agile hunter of insects and small invertebrates.
funFact: The green crested lizard is often mistaken for a chameleon because it can shift from vivid green to dark brown when stressed — but unlike true chameleons, it has no special colour-change cells and does this through simple pigment redistribution.

name: Sun Skink
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Will flee if approached.
description: The many-lined sun skink is one of the most commonly seen lizards across Southeast Asia, a robust, glossy-scaled skink that loves to bask in sunny patches on logs, rocks, and footpaths. Named for its habit of sunbathing, it has a brown back with pale lateral stripes and a copper-orange flush to the flanks. A quick, alert predator of insects and small invertebrates, it retreats rapidly into leaf litter or undergrowth at the first sign of danger.
funFact: Sun skinks are one of the few skink species in the region that give birth to live young rather than laying eggs — retaining developing embryos internally until they are fully formed.

name: Oriental Whip Snake
dangerNotes: Rear-fanged and mildly venomous but not medically significant to humans. Bites are very rare. Harmless in practice.
description: The oriental whip snake is an extraordinarily slender arboreal snake, so thin relative to its length that it resembles a green vine or tendril hanging among foliage. Vivid lime-green with a pointed snout, it moves slowly and deliberately through vegetation hunting lizards and frogs. It has horizontally keyhole-shaped pupils that give it excellent binocular vision — unusually precise for a snake — allowing it to judge distance when striking from a branch.
funFact: The oriental whip snake has keyhole-shaped horizontal pupils that give it binocular depth perception — one of the very few snakes capable of genuinely judging distance, a crucial adaptation for striking at prey from branches.

name: Crab-eating Macaque
dangerNotes: Can bite and scratch. Carries Herpes B virus (potentially fatal to humans). Highly opportunistic — will snatch food, bags, and glasses. Do not feed. Do not make eye contact with dominant males.
description: The crab-eating macaque, also known as the long-tailed macaque, is the most commonly encountered primate across Southeast Asia — ubiquitous at temples, beach resorts, forest parks, and coastal areas. Despite its name, it eats almost anything: crabs, fruit, insects, small animals, and human food. Highly intelligent and socially complex, it lives in troops with rigid dominance hierarchies. Its boldness and adaptability have made it both a cultural icon and an urban nuisance.
funFact: Crab-eating macaques in Thailand and Myanmar have been observed using stone tools to crack open shellfish and nuts — one of the few non-ape primates documented using tools in the wild.

name: Asian Palm Civet
dangerNotes: Nocturnal and reclusive. Will scratch and bite if cornered. Otherwise avoids humans.
description: The Asian palm civet is a small, cat-like carnivore with a dark grizzled coat, black mask, and pale-spotted flanks. Highly adaptable, it thrives in forest, plantation, and suburban environments across Southeast Asia. Primarily frugivorous, it plays an important role in seed dispersal. It is also, controversially, the source of kopi luwak — coffee made from beans passed through its digestive system — the world's most expensive coffee.
funFact: The Asian palm civet is responsible for kopi luwak, the world's most expensive coffee — it eats ripe coffee cherries and the beans, partially digested and fermented in its gut, are collected, cleaned, and sold for up to $700 per kilogram.

name: Common Treeshrew
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Extremely shy and fast — rarely seen closely.
description: The common treeshrew resembles a small squirrel with a pointed snout, but is not a rodent — it belongs to the order Scandentia, considered one of the closest living relatives of primates. Hyperactive and diurnal, it dashes along branches and forest floors at high speed, foraging for insects, fruit, and small vertebrates. Despite its name, it spends much of its time on the ground. Its remarkably high metabolic rate means it must eat almost constantly.
funFact: Treeshrews have the highest brain-to-body-mass ratio of any mammal — higher even than humans — though this reflects their tiny body size rather than exceptional intelligence.

name: White-throated Kingfisher
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The white-throated kingfisher is one of the most conspicuous and boldly coloured birds of Southeast Asia, with a vivid turquoise back and wings, chestnut head and flanks, and a brilliant white throat and breast. Unusually for a kingfisher, it hunts far from water — perching on telephone wires, fence posts, and roof edges to dive on lizards, large insects, frogs, and even small rodents. Its loud, laughing call is a defining sound of the tropical dawn.
funFact: Despite being called a kingfisher, the white-throated kingfisher often lives far from water and regularly hunts lizards, insects, and rodents in dry urban gardens — it is named for its family, not its diet.

name: Collared Kingfisher
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The collared kingfisher is one of the most widespread kingfishers in the world, ranging from the Red Sea to the Pacific. In Southeast Asia it is a constant presence in mangroves, coastal parks, and urban gardens. Blue-green above with a crisp white collar and underparts, it hunts from a prominent perch, diving on crabs, mudskippers, lizards, and large insects. Its loud, harsh 'kek-kek-kek' call rings out constantly across mangrove-fringed coastlines.
funFact: The collared kingfisher has one of the widest distributions of any kingfisher in the world — 49 recognised subspecies spread from the Red Sea coast to the islands of the Pacific Ocean.

name: Asian Koel
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The Asian koel is one of the most heard but rarely seen birds of Southeast Asia. The male is glossy jet black with a vivid red eye; the female is beautifully streaked brown. A brood parasite, the koel lays its eggs in the nests of crows and other large birds, leaving the hosts to raise its chicks. The male's rising, repetitive 'ko-el' call — accelerating in pitch through the dawn hours — is an iconic and sometimes maddening sound of tropical cities.
funFact: The Asian koel's call has been scientifically proven to accelerate in tempo and pitch over the breeding season — a vocal performance that can begin before dawn and continue relentlessly for hours, making it both beloved and infamous in equal measure.

name: Oriental Magpie-Robin
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The oriental magpie-robin is one of the finest songbirds in Southeast Asia — a small, bold black-and-white bird that delivers an extraordinarily rich and varied song from exposed perches, often at dawn. Males have a glossy blue-black head and back with white underparts and wing patches; females are grey-brown. Highly territorial, males sing persistently throughout the breeding season. It is the national bird of Bangladesh and deeply familiar across urban Southeast Asia.
funFact: The oriental magpie-robin is one of the most accomplished songbirds in Asia — males can produce over 50 distinct song phrases and frequently incorporate imitations of other species into their dawn chorus.

name: Olive-backed Sunbird
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The olive-backed sunbird is the most widespread and commonly seen sunbird in Southeast Asia, a tiny, restless nectarivore with an olive-green back and sulphur-yellow underparts. Males have a brilliant iridescent blue-black throat and breast. It hovers briefly or clings acrobatically to flowers to feed on nectar, and is an important pollinator across the region. It builds a distinctive hanging, pendulous nest of grass and spiders' webs suspended from branches or even laundry lines.
funFact: The olive-backed sunbird will happily build its hanging, pendulous nest from a washing line, a light fitting, or a clothes hanger — making it one of the most urban-adapted nesting birds in Southeast Asia.

name: Black-naped Oriole
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The black-naped oriole is a strikingly beautiful bird — vivid golden yellow with a black mask and nape band. One of the most conspicuous garden birds across urban Southeast Asia, it is often seen in fruiting trees and flowering canopy. Its rich, fluting whistle is one of the most melodious and instantly recognisable bird calls in the region. Adaptable to urban environments, it nests in a woven cup suspended hammock-like from a high branch.
funFact: The black-naped oriole's fluting call is one of the most melodious sounds in Southeast Asian gardens — it can be confused with a human whistling, and individuals are known to incorporate other bird calls and even human-made sounds into their song.

name: Blue-tailed Bee-eater
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The blue-tailed bee-eater is a vivid, acrobatic bird with green plumage, a rufous-orange throat, blue tail streamers, and a long decurved bill. It hunts bees, wasps, dragonflies, and other flying insects with spectacular aerial precision, catching them in mid-air and returning to a perch to beat and de-venom prey before swallowing. A gregarious, migratory species, it breeds in sandy banks and open ground and is a seasonal visitor across much of Southeast Asia.
funFact: Blue-tailed bee-eaters catch bees and wasps mid-flight then thrash them against a branch to remove the sting and squeeze out the venom sac before eating — a learned behaviour that prevents envenomation.

name: Brahminy Kite
dangerNotes: No threat to humans on the ground. May swoop if nesting nearby.
description: The brahminy kite is one of the most beautiful raptors in Southeast Asia — a medium-sized bird of prey with a pure white head and chest contrasting vividly with rich chestnut-red wings and back. A coastal and wetland specialist, it soars effortlessly over harbours, estuaries, and fishing villages, snatching dead fish, crabs, and carrion from the water surface. In Hindu mythology it represents Garuda, the vehicle of the god Vishnu.
funFact: The brahminy kite is considered a manifestation of the Hindu deity Garuda across much of Southeast Asia — it is a sacred bird in Bali, where it is believed to carry messages from the gods.

name: Black-shouldered Kite
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The black-shouldered kite is a small, elegant raptor with pale grey-white plumage, jet black shoulder patches, and striking red eyes. It hunts by hovering in place over open grassland — facing into the wind and scanning the ground below with exceptional eyesight before dropping onto rodents and large insects. Increasingly common across agricultural Southeast Asia, it benefits from open farmland where it is a highly effective rat predator.
funFact: The black-shouldered kite can hover almost perfectly stationary against the wind, maintaining position for up to a minute using tiny, rapid wingbeats and tail adjustments — a hunting technique called 'kiting'.

name: Rose-ringed Parakeet
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Noisy in large flocks.
description: The rose-ringed parakeet is a long-tailed green parrot with a distinctive red bill and, in males, a black-and-rose neck ring. One of the most successful introduced birds in the world, it has established wild populations across Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia from escaped cage birds. Intelligent, adaptable, and noisy, feral flocks roost communally in large numbers and can be agricultural pests. In Southeast Asia both native and introduced populations exist.
funFact: The rose-ringed parakeet is one of the most invasive bird species on Earth — escaped cage birds have established self-sustaining wild populations in over 35 countries, including the UK, where London now has over 12,000 wild individuals.

name: Red-breasted Parakeet
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The red-breasted parakeet is one of the most attractive parakeets in Southeast Asia, with grey-green plumage, a salmon-pink breast, black chin stripe, and red upper bill. It inhabits forest, plantations, and increasingly urban areas. Males and females are distinguishable — females have a dull reddish lower mandible while males have red upper and black lower. Highly gregarious, it roosts and forages in noisy, fast-flying flocks and is a popular cage bird.
funFact: The red-breasted parakeet can be reliably sexed by bill colour alone — males have a red upper mandible with black lower, while females have a fully dull reddish bill on both upper and lower.

name: Greater Coucal
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The greater coucal is a large, crow-sized member of the cuckoo family with glossy blue-black plumage and rich chestnut-red wings. Unlike most cuckoos, it raises its own young rather than parasitising other birds. A slow, heavy bird that prefers to walk through dense undergrowth, it hunts lizards, large insects, eggs, and small rodents. Its deep, resonant 'boop-boop-boop' call is one of the most characteristic sounds of rural Southeast Asia.
funFact: Unlike most of its cuckoo relatives, the greater coucal builds its own nest and raises its own young — making it one of the few members of the cuckoo family that is not a brood parasite.

name: Spotted Dove
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The spotted dove is one of the most familiar and widespread birds of urban Southeast Asia, a pinkish-brown dove with a distinctive black-and-white spotted neck patch. It walks calmly on the ground foraging for seeds, completely untroubled by human presence. Its gentle, repetitive cooing — 'coo-coo-coo-coo' — is a constant background sound of tropical gardens and city parks. Introduced to Australia, Hawaii, and many other regions, it has become an established alien species.
funFact: Spotted doves, like all pigeons and doves, produce 'crop milk' — a protein-rich secretion from the lining of the crop that both parents feed to newly hatched squabs before they can digest solid food.

name: Zebra Dove
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The zebra dove is a tiny, delicately barred dove with fine black-and-white streaking on its neck and breast that resembles a zebra's stripes — giving it its name. One of the most abundant birds in urban Southeast Asia, it walks along pavements, garden paths, and outdoor café tables with total confidence. Its soft, rapid cooing is one of the most soothing sounds of the tropical dawn. It is extremely popular as a caged songbird in Thailand and Malaysia.
funFact: The zebra dove is so prized as a caged songbird in Thailand and Malaysia that competitive calling contests are held, with champion birds worth thousands of dollars — judges score their distinctive rapid cooing on duration, tone, and rhythm.

name: Rhesus Macaque
dangerNotes: Can bite and scratch. Carries Herpes B virus (potentially fatal to humans). Do not feed or approach. Common at temples.
description: The rhesus macaque is one of the most widespread and adaptable primates in Asia, equally at home in forests, farmland, and busy urban centres. Highly social and intelligent, they live in troops of 20–200 individuals with complex dominance hierarchies. They are famous in Thailand for the annual Monkey Buffet Festival in Lopburi, where hundreds gather to feast on fruit.
funFact: Rhesus macaques were among the first primates sent to space — Able and Miss Baker made history in 1959 aboard a US rocket.

name: Flat-tailed House Gecko
dangerNotes: Completely harmless to humans. Beneficial insect predator in homes.
description: The flat-tailed house gecko is one of the most familiar reptiles in Southeast Asia, a constant presence on the walls and ceilings of homes, hotels, and restaurants after dark. Its distinctive flattened body and tail allow it to squeeze into the thinnest crevices. Using millions of microscopic hair-like setae on its toes, it can walk upside down on any surface. A welcome guest, it devours mosquitoes, moths, and other insects.
funFact: House geckos can detach their tails when grabbed by predators — the tail continues to wriggle as a distraction while the gecko escapes. A new tail, made of cartilage, regrows within weeks.

name: Green Tree Skink
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Will flee immediately if approached.
description: The olive tree skink is a sleek, shiny lizard with smooth overlapping scales and a long tapering tail. An excellent climber, it spends most of its life in trees and shrubs, hunting insects and small invertebrates. Its olive-green to bronze colouring provides camouflage against bark and leaves. When threatened it moves with surprising speed, vanishing into bark crevices or dense foliage.
funFact: Skink scales contain tiny crystals within their structure that produce a characteristic iridescent shimmer — more pronounced in some species than others.

name: Crested Lizard
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. May puff up and gape as a bluff display.
description: The crested lizard is a common agamid found throughout Thailand's gardens, parks, and forest edges. Males sport a distinctive raised crest along the neck and back and display vivid colour changes — flushing red-orange around the head — during territorial or courtship displays. An active predator of insects, it bobs its head rhythmically as a territorial signal. Closely related to the widespread garden lizard (Calotes versicolor).
funFact: Male crested lizards can change the colour of their head from dull brown to vivid red within seconds during territorial confrontations — a faster colour change than a chameleon.

name: White-lipped Pit Viper
dangerNotes: Venomous. Causes severe local tissue damage, pain, and swelling. Bites occasionally fatal. Highly camouflaged in green foliage — look carefully before reaching into vegetation. A common cause of snakebite in Thailand.
description: The white-lipped pit viper is a small, vivid green arboreal viper and one of the most common venomous snakes encountered in Thailand. Females are larger than males and may be green or brownish. It hunts from ambush at night, detecting warm-blooded prey with heat-sensitive pit organs between eye and nostril. Despite its small size, its haemotoxic venom causes significant tissue damage and can be life-threatening.
funFact: Pit vipers have an infrared-sensing pit organ that can detect temperature differences as small as 0.003°C — effectively giving them thermal imaging to locate prey in complete darkness.

name: Golden Tree Snake
dangerNotes: Mildly venomous (rear-fanged) but venom is not medically significant to humans. Bites are extremely rare. Harmless to humans.
description: The golden tree snake is one of Southeast Asia's most beautiful and acrobatic reptiles, patterned in vivid green and black scales with golden flecks. One of the world's few genuinely flying snakes, it can launch itself from a branch, flatten its body into a concave S-shape to trap air, and glide up to 10 metres between trees. Fast, agile, and diurnal, it hunts lizards and geckos high in the forest canopy.
funFact: The golden tree snake 'flies' by flattening its entire body and undulating in S-curves — effectively turning itself into a living wing that can glide and even steer in mid-air.

name: Copperhead Racer
dangerNotes: Non-venomous but large and aggressive when cornered. Can deliver a painful bite and may coil and strike repeatedly. Keep distance.
description: The copperhead racer is a large, fast, and feisty colubrid snake with a distinctive copper-red head, cream underside, and dark-striped body. One of the most commonly encountered large snakes in Thailand's disturbed habitats and agricultural areas. Non-venomous but quick-tempered — if cornered it will flatten its body, vibrate its tail, and strike repeatedly. An excellent predator of rodents, making it ecologically valuable on farmland.
funFact: The copperhead racer can move at impressive speed through grass and undergrowth — in pursuit of prey it has been clocked at over 3 metres per second in short bursts.

name: Indochinese Ratsnake
dangerNotes: Non-venomous. Very fast and will flee rather than bite. Occasional defensive strike if cornered — bite is harmless.
description: The Indo-Chinese ratsnake is a slender, fast-moving colubrid and one of the most commonly seen large snakes in Thailand. With a smooth olive-brown back and pale yellow underside, it is a generalist predator of rodents, frogs, and lizards across a huge range of habitats. An excellent swimmer and climber, it is often found near water. Highly beneficial to farmers as a natural rodent controller.
funFact: Indochinese ratsnakes have been recorded climbing vertical walls and crossing roads at speed — their long, muscular build makes them among the fastest snakes in Thailand.

name: Monocled Cobra
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Potent neurotoxic and cytotoxic venom causes paralysis and tissue destruction — bites are frequently fatal without treatment. Spreads a broad hood when threatened. Seek emergency care immediately if bitten.
description: The monocled cobra is one of the most medically significant snakes in Southeast Asia, responsible for a large proportion of serious snakebite cases across the region. Named for the distinctive O-shaped or monocle marking on the back of its hood, it inhabits agricultural land, forest edges, and is regularly found near villages. Unlike the spitting cobra, it does not spit venom, but its bite delivers a potent combination of neurotoxins and cytotoxins.
funFact: The monocled cobra's distinctive hood marking — a single O-shaped 'eye' on the back — is thought to function as a false face to confuse and deter predators approaching from behind.

name: Reticulated Python
dangerNotes: The world's longest snake — adults regularly exceed 5 metres and have killed humans by constriction. Never approach large individuals alone. Even mid-sized adults are capable of serious injury. Back away and do not provoke.
description: The reticulated python is the world's longest snake, with verified individuals exceeding 6 metres and unverified records beyond 8. Its intricate golden, black, and white geometric patterning — the 'reticulation' — gives it its name. Supremely adaptable, it inhabits rainforest, mangroves, and urban drains alike, and is a regular visitor to suburban areas across Southeast Asia. A powerful ambush predator, it has on rare occasions killed and swallowed adult humans.
funFact: The reticulated python holds the record for the world's longest snake — a specimen from Indonesia measured at 7.67 metres, and local accounts of individuals exceeding 8 metres are considered credible.

name: Sunda Flying Lemur
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Nocturnal and arboreal — very rarely encountered.
description: The Sunda flying lemur — also called the colugo — is neither a lemur nor capable of true flight, but its gliding membrane (patagium) stretches from its chin to the tips of its fingers, toes, and tail, giving it the most complete gliding surface of any gliding mammal. It can glide over 136 metres between trees with minimal altitude loss. Despite its superficial resemblance to lemurs, it is most closely related to primates — our nearest non-primate relative.
funFact: The Sunda flying lemur can glide over 136 metres in a single leap with a height loss of less than 10 metres — a gliding efficiency that exceeds flying squirrels and rivalled only by true bats among nocturnal mammals.

name: Oriental Pied Hornbill
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The oriental pied hornbill is the smallest and most widespread hornbill in Southeast Asia, with bold black-and-white plumage and a large yellow-and-black casque atop its bill. Famous for its extraordinary nesting behaviour: the female seals herself inside a tree cavity using mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit through which the male passes food, until the chicks are ready to fledge. A noisy, social bird, its loud cackling calls are characteristic of forest edges and offshore islands.
funFact: Female hornbills seal themselves inside tree hollows during nesting — entombed with their eggs and then chicks for up to four months while the male feeds them through a narrow slit, making them entirely dependent on their partner's fidelity.

name: Sun Conure
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Wild SEA populations are escaped captive birds.
description: The sun conure is a brilliantly coloured parrot native to northeastern South America, with vivid golden-yellow plumage shading to orange-red on the face and green on the wings. In Southeast Asia all wild individuals are escaped or released captive birds — the species is not native to the region. Highly social and extremely noisy, escaped flocks have established themselves in urban parks across Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. In its native range it is endangered due to trapping for the pet trade.
funFact: Every sun conure seen in the wild across Southeast Asia is descended from escaped or released pets — the species is not native to Asia but has established feral flocks in several major cities.

name: Banded Bay Cuckoo
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The banded bay cuckoo is a small, secretive cuckoo with rufous-brown upperparts and a finely barred white underside. A brood parasite like its relatives, it lays its eggs in the nests of babblers and other small birds, whose own chicks it displaces. Heard far more often than seen, its distinctive plaintive, descending four-note whistle is a characteristic sound of Southeast Asian forest edges during the breeding season.
funFact: Cuckoo chicks hatch earlier than their hosts' own eggs and instinctively eject all other eggs from the nest within hours of hatching — blind, naked, and just hours old, they perform this behaviour with remarkable precision.

name: Stump-tailed Macaque
dangerNotes: Stocky and powerful. Can bite severely if threatened. Do not approach in the wild.
description: The stump-tailed macaque is a stocky, ground-dwelling primate recognisable by its bare red face and vestigial tail. Found in dense montane and lowland forests of northern Thailand, it is more terrestrial than other macaques. Adults develop vivid red or pink facial colouring that deepens with age and social status. Populations are declining due to habitat loss and hunting.
funFact: Stump-tailed macaques have one of the most complex grooming repertoires of any macaque species, spending hours maintaining social bonds through mutual grooming.

name: Pig-tailed Macaque
dangerNotes: Strong and can bite aggressively if provoked. Trained individuals used in coconut harvesting are often stressed and unpredictable.
description: Named for its short, erect, curled tail resembling a pig's, the pig-tailed macaque is a large, powerful primate of lowland rainforests in southern Thailand. It spends more time on the ground than most macaques, foraging across forest floors. In parts of Thailand and Malaysia, individuals are controversially trained to climb and harvest coconuts from tall palms.
funFact: Wild pig-tailed macaques have been observed acting as apex predators in some forest systems, actively hunting and killing other smaller animals including slow lorises.

name: Dusky Langur
dangerNotes: Shy and non-aggressive. Will retreat from humans. No significant danger.
description: The dusky langur is a slender, long-tailed leaf monkey with distinctive white eye rings that give it a permanently wide-eyed, spectacled look. Common on Thailand's limestone hill forests and in Penang, Malaysia, it lives in small groups and feeds almost entirely on leaves and unripe fruit. Infants are born a brilliant orange colour, turning dark grey within months.
funFact: Dusky langur infants are born bright orange — a colour thought to attract communal care from all females in the troop, not just the mother.

name: Silvered Langur
dangerNotes: Shy and arboreal. No threat to humans.
description: The silvered langur, named for the silver-tipped hairs that give its dark coat a frosted shimmer, is a slender leaf monkey of coastal and riverine forests. An agile climber, it rarely descends to the ground. Like other langurs, it has a specialised multi-chambered stomach to ferment and digest large quantities of tough leaves. Infants are vivid orange, turning silver-grey within a few months.
funFact: Silvered langurs have enlarged salivary glands and a complex stomach similar to a cow's to help neutralise the toxins in the leaves they eat.

name: Giant Flying Squirrel
dangerNotes: Nocturnal and shy. Poses no threat to humans.
description: The giant flying squirrel is the largest of all flying squirrels, with a body up to 58 cm long and a gliding membrane (patagium) stretching from wrist to ankle. Rather than flying, it glides between trees — covering distances of up to 100 metres in a single leap — using its bushy tail to steer. A strictly nocturnal forest animal, it feeds on fruit, leaves, and bark.
funFact: Giant flying squirrels can glide over 100 metres in a single leap, losing very little altitude due to their extraordinarily large gliding membrane.

name: Common Porcupine
dangerNotes: Quills can lodge painfully in flesh and cause infection. Will charge backwards if threatened. Do not corner.
description: The Malayan porcupine is the largest rodent in Thailand, covered in a formidable armour of black-and-white spines up to 35 cm long. A nocturnal burrower, it shelters in caves or self-dug dens during the day. Porcupines rattle their quills as a warning and will reverse rapidly into a threat if it persists. They gnaw bones for calcium, often collecting them at den sites.
funFact: Porcupine quills are loosely attached and will detach on contact — they are not 'shot' at predators, but can work their way deeper into flesh due to tiny backward-facing barbs.

name: Golden Jackal
dangerNotes: Rarely aggressive toward humans but can carry rabies. Avoid contact.
description: The golden jackal is a medium-sized canid and one of the most adaptable members of the dog family, expanding its range more rapidly than almost any other carnivore. In Thailand it is found in open habitats and forest edges. An opportunistic omnivore, it eats everything from fruit and insects to carrion and small mammals. Pairs mate for life and cooperate to raise pups and defend territory.
funFact: Golden jackals are rapidly expanding westward into Europe — they have been recorded in Germany, the Netherlands, and even Norway in recent decades.

name: Large Indian Civet
dangerNotes: Nocturnal and secretive. May spray a musky secretion if threatened. No significant danger.
description: The large Indian civet is a long-bodied, short-legged carnivore with bold black-and-white striped flanks and a banded tail. A secretive, solitary nocturnal hunter, it forages on the forest floor for small animals, eggs, fruits, and carrion. Scent glands near its tail produce a strong musky secretion called civetone, historically harvested for perfume production.
funFact: Civet musk was one of the most prized ingredients in luxury perfumes for centuries — including early formulations of Chanel No. 5 — until synthetic alternatives were developed.

name: Small Indian Civet
dangerNotes: Avoids humans. Will emit foul musk if cornered. No significant danger.
description: The small Indian civet is a slender, cat-sized carnivore with spotted sides and a long ringed tail. More adaptable than its larger relative, it thrives in degraded habitats, agricultural land, and even near villages. Solitary and nocturnal, it hunts rodents, birds, insects, and reptiles. Like all civets, it marks territory extensively using scent glands.
funFact: The small Indian civet was introduced to Madagascar and the Comoro Islands centuries ago, likely by Arab traders who valued its musk.

name: Yellow-throated Marten
dangerNotes: Bold but avoids humans. Can bite if handled. No significant threat.
description: The yellow-throated marten is the largest marten in Asia and one of the most visually striking, with a dark chocolate body, vivid yellow-orange throat and chest, and a long bushy tail. Unlike most mustelids, it is often active during the day and hunts cooperatively in pairs or small groups — one of the few mustelids to do so. It is fast, agile, and capable of killing prey much larger than itself, including muntjac deer.
funFact: Yellow-throated martens are known to follow packs of dholes and steal scraps from their kills — a bold strategy given the dhole's ferocity.

name: Mouse Deer
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Extremely shy and will flee instantly.
description: The lesser mouse deer is the world's smallest hoofed mammal, no bigger than a rabbit. Despite resembling a tiny deer, it belongs to an ancient family (Tragulidae) that has remained virtually unchanged for 30 million years — earning it the title of a living fossil. It lacks antlers but males have small protruding upper canine tusks used in fights. An exquisitely shy forest animal, it freezes and then bolts at the slightest disturbance.
funFact: Mouse deer are the world's smallest hoofed mammals, but males settle disputes using canine tusks rather than antlers, like miniature musk deer.

name: Smooth-coated Otter
dangerNotes: Will bite if cornered or if pups are threatened. Generally avoids humans.
description: The smooth-coated otter is the largest otter in Southeast Asia, named for its unusually short, velvety fur. It lives in family groups of up to 11 individuals and hunts cooperatively, herding fish into shallow water. Highly vocal, family members maintain contact with a range of calls including chirps, squeaks, and loud screams. It is closely tied to large rivers and estuaries and is increasingly threatened by wetland destruction.
funFact: Smooth-coated otters hunt cooperatively — family groups fan out in the water and herd fish together, then dive simultaneously for an efficient group catch.

name: Asian Small-clawed Otter
dangerNotes: Gentle but may nip if stressed. Increasingly popular but poorly suited as a pet.
description: The Asian small-clawed otter is the world's smallest otter, distinguished by its partially webbed feet with tiny, peg-like claws rather than the full claws of other species. This adaptation allows remarkable dexterity — they manipulate prey by hand rather than using their mouth. They live in extended family groups and are famously playful. Sadly their popularity as exotic pets is a significant conservation threat.
funFact: Asian small-clawed otters use their highly dextrous paws to feel for and catch crabs, molluscs, and frogs in muddy water without needing to see their prey.

name: Eurasian Otter
dangerNotes: Shy and rarely seen. Will bite if cornered. Generally avoids humans.
description: The Eurasian otter has the widest range of any otter species, extending from Ireland to Southeast Asia. In Thailand it occupies clean mountain rivers and streams. A solitary, mostly nocturnal predator, it is superbly adapted for aquatic life with webbed feet, a tapering muscular tail for steering, and the ability to close its ears and nostrils underwater. It marks territory extensively using spraints (droppings) with a distinctive musky smell.
funFact: Eurasian otters can remain underwater for up to four minutes and can dive to depths of 10–12 metres to catch fish.

name: Common Gliding Lizard
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Virtually never approached closely in the wild.
description: The common gliding lizard is a small agamid that has evolved a remarkable gliding apparatus: elongated ribs that can splay outward, stretching a thin membrane of skin on each flank into wings. Males display vivid yellow-orange throat fans and wing markings. They glide between trees to forage for ants and defend territory, achieving distances of up to 9 metres with precise control. Females descend to the forest floor only to lay eggs.
funFact: Male Draco lizards have territory so precisely defended that they know the exact flight path between their home trees — they will glide the same route dozens of times per day.

name: Malayan Flying Lizard
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The Malayan flying lizard is closely related to the common gliding lizard and shares its extraordinary gliding ability using wing-like skin flaps stretched over elongated ribs. Found in lowland and hill forests of southern Thailand, males have bluish gliding membranes and a yellow-orange throat fan used in display. Both species feed almost exclusively on ants and termites harvested from tree trunks.
funFact: Flying lizards are so specialised for arboreal life that females find descending to lay eggs so risky they spend the minimum possible time on the ground — often less than 30 minutes total.

name: Water Dragon
dangerNotes: Harmless in the wild. May scratch or whip its tail defensively. Popular in the pet trade.
description: The Chinese water dragon is a large, brilliantly coloured agamid with vivid green scales, a high crest along neck and back, and a long banded tail that makes up two-thirds of its total length. Always found near water, it basks on branches overhanging rivers and dives in at the first sign of danger — it can remain submerged for up to 25 minutes. Highly sought after in the international pet trade.
funFact: Water dragons can hold their breath for up to 25 minutes underwater to escape predators, lying motionless on the riverbed.

name: Indochinese Spitting Cobra
dangerNotes: Highly dangerous. Can spit venom accurately up to 2.5 metres, causing severe eye damage and potential blindness. Bite is potentially fatal — seek emergency care immediately. Never approach.
description: The Siamese spitting cobra is Thailand's most medically significant cobra, capable of both delivering a potentially fatal bite and spitting venom with extraordinary accuracy. It spreads a broad hood when threatened. Colouration varies from grey to brown to black with lighter bands. Common on agricultural land where it hunts rodents, frogs, and other snakes. Responsible for many snakebite cases in Thailand annually.
funFact: Spitting cobras aim for the eyes with remarkable accuracy, spitting two jets of venom that converge at the target — they can hit a 2 cm target at 2 metres while the target is moving.

name: Banded Krait
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Powerful neurotoxic venom causes respiratory failure. Often docile by day but active and more aggressive at night. Bites may be initially painless, delaying treatment — fatal if untreated. Seek emergency care immediately.
description: The banded krait is a large, strikingly patterned snake with alternating bold yellow and black bands. Though often sluggish and reluctant to bite during the day, it becomes active and significantly more dangerous after dark. Its potent neurotoxic venom blocks nerve signals to muscles, causing progressive paralysis and potentially fatal respiratory failure. It feeds primarily on other snakes. One of Asia's most dangerous snakes.
funFact: Banded kraits are so reluctant to bite during daylight that they will allow themselves to be handled without striking — but this docility completely disappears after dark.

name: Malayan Krait
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Neurotoxic venom is more potent than most cobras. Bites are often painless, causing victims to delay seeking help — a major reason bites are frequently fatal. Seek emergency care immediately.
description: The Malayan krait is one of the most dangerous snakes in Southeast Asia, responsible for a disproportionate number of fatalities relative to its encounter frequency. It has black and white bands and a slender body, and it enters houses at night in pursuit of geckos and rodents. Its neurotoxic venom is highly potent and bites are often painless, leading victims to underestimate the severity of envenomation until paralysis sets in.
funFact: The Malayan krait's venom contains unique toxins that attack synapses in the nervous system irreversibly — even antivenom cannot reverse the damage once paralysis begins, making immediate treatment critical.

name: Malayan Pit Viper
dangerNotes: One of the leading causes of snakebite death in Southeast Asia. Perfectly camouflaged in leaf litter — easily stepped on. Long fangs deliver a powerful haemotoxic venom causing tissue destruction, clotting disorders, and organ failure. Seek emergency care immediately.
description: The Malayan pit viper is responsible for more snakebite deaths than any other snake in Southeast Asia. Superbly camouflaged in brown, grey, and pink leaf-litter patterns, it lies motionless on the forest floor waiting in ambush. Sluggish during the day, it becomes active and quick-striking at night. Its long, hinged fangs deliver a potent haemotoxic venom causing devastating local tissue necrosis, coagulopathy, and potential kidney failure.
funFact: The Malayan pit viper was the first snake from which the anticoagulant drug ancrod was derived — its venom proteins are still studied for potential cardiovascular medications.

name: Wagler's Pit Viper
dangerNotes: Venomous. Causes pain, swelling, and local tissue damage. Rarely fatal but requires medical attention. Famous for inhabiting the Snake Temple in Penang.
description: Wagler's pit viper is a heavy-bodied, slow-moving arboreal viper with striking sexual dimorphism — females are large with vivid green and yellow patterns; males are much smaller and darker. It spends most of its life draped motionless over branches, relying on camouflage rather than escape. In Penang, Malaysia, hundreds inhabit a Buddhist temple where they are considered sacred and live in the incense smoke.
funFact: Wagler's pit vipers at the Snake Temple in Penang are so accustomed to human presence and incense smoke that they become lethargic and rarely strike, despite being fully venomous.

name: Paradise Tree Snake
dangerNotes: Rear-fanged and very mildly venomous. No risk to humans. Extremely unlikely to bite.
description: The paradise tree snake is the most accomplished gliding snake in the world, capable of gliding up to 10 metres and even making mid-air turns. Its vivid black scales with red, orange, and green spots make it unmistakable. Like its relative the golden tree snake, it launches from heights and undulates its flattened body to generate lift. Found in southern Thailand's rainforests, it hunts lizards and geckos in the canopy.
funFact: Studies show the paradise tree snake is a better glider than any flying squirrel relative to body size — it loses very little altitude over distance and can actively steer in mid-flight.

name: Sunbeam Snake
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Fossorial and avoids contact. May musk if handled.
description: The sunbeam snake is a secretive, burrowing snake famed for its extraordinary iridescence — in direct sunlight, its smooth dark scales refract light into a shifting rainbow of colour across the entire body. It spends most of its life underground in moist soil, emerging at night to hunt frogs, lizards, and small rodents. A primitive snake with vestigial hind limb remnants, it belongs to one of the most ancient snake families.
funFact: The sunbeam snake's scales contain a microscopic layered structure that diffracts light into a full spectrum of colour — each scale acts like a tiny prism.

name: Pipe Snake
dangerNotes: Completely non-venomous. When threatened, it hides its head and raises its bright red tail as a decoy — mimicking a dangerous snake. Harmless.
description: The red-tailed pipe snake is a small, cylindrical burrowing snake with a blunt head and a short, bright red underside to its tail. When threatened, it employs a remarkable defence — hiding its vulnerable head under its coils while raising and flattening its red-tipped tail to mimic a cobra head, deterring predators. A primitive snake with vestigial pelvic girdle remnants, it feeds primarily on caecilians and other elongate prey underground.
funFact: The pipe snake's tail-as-false-head display is so convincing that even experienced herpetologists have been briefly fooled — the tail is the same width as the head and flattens to mimic a cobra hood.

name: Dog-toothed Cat Snake
dangerNotes: Rear-fanged with very mild venom. Not medically significant to humans. May bite defensively.
description: The dog-toothed cat snake is one of the largest cat snakes, named for its unusually large, fang-like teeth at the front of the mouth used to grip and subdue prey. A slender, highly compressed arboreal snake, it hunts birds, lizards, and small mammals in the forest canopy at night. Large eyes with vertical pupils give excellent low-light vision. Its rear-fanged venom is effective on prey but poses no significant risk to humans.
funFact: Cat snakes have a vertical pupil similar to a cat's — which dilates enormously in low light, giving them excellent night vision for hunting in the dark forest canopy.

name: Mangrove Cat Snake
dangerNotes: Rear-fanged, mildly venomous. Not dangerous to humans. Can bite defensively — has a feisty temperament.
description: The gold-ringed cat snake is one of Southeast Asia's most visually striking serpents — jet black with vivid yellow or gold bands encircling the body. A large arboreal specialist of mangrove and lowland forest, it is an active nocturnal hunter of birds, lizards, frogs, and small mammals. Despite its menacing appearance, its rear-fanged venom poses no serious risk to humans, though it has a defensive temperament and will bite if handled.
funFact: The mangrove cat snake's bold yellow-black banding mimics the colouration of genuinely dangerous banded kraits — a case of Batesian mimicry that deters predators.

name: Striped Kukri Snake
dangerNotes: Non-venomous. Enlarged rear teeth may cause minor lacerations. Completely harmless.
description: The striped kukri snake is a small, slender colubrid named for its enlarged, curved rear teeth resembling kukri blades — used to slash and extract contents from reptile eggs, its speciality prey. Brown with dark stripes, it is a secretive ground-dweller found in drier forests and scrubland. Though completely harmless, it may bleed from the mouth when biting due to the placement of its unusual dentition.
funFact: Kukri snakes specialise in eating reptile eggs — their distinctive curved rear teeth are used to cut open the egg while it is still inside the nest, then consume the contents in situ.

name: Malayan Forest Gecko
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The Malayan bent-toed gecko is a slender, long-toed forest gecko with banded brown and cream patterning. Unlike house geckos, it lacks the adhesive toe pads and instead has long, curved claws for gripping bark and rock. Found on forest floors and limestone outcrops, it is a secretive nocturnal hunter of small invertebrates. One of many gecko species in a complex that includes numerous near-identical-looking relatives.
funFact: Unlike their wall-climbing relatives, bent-toed geckos have clawed feet rather than adhesive pads — they navigate rough bark and rock by gripping rather than sticking.

name: Asian Leaf Turtle
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. May bite weakly if handled.
description: The Asian leaf turtle is a medium-sized semi-aquatic turtle with a low, rounded, brown-to-olive shell that closely resembles a dead leaf — excellent camouflage on the forest floor. A unique feature is its partially hinged lower shell (plastron), which allows partial closure like a box turtle. Found in slow-moving forest streams and swamps, it eats a wide variety of plant and animal matter. Heavily exploited for food and the pet trade.
funFact: Young Asian leaf turtles have a keel running down the shell that flattens as they age — hatchlings look almost like a different species to the smooth-shelled adults.

name: Leopard Cat
dangerNotes: Wild individuals will flee from humans. Will scratch and bite if cornered or handled.
description: The leopard cat is the most widespread small wild cat in Asia, roughly the size of a domestic cat but with a beautifully spotted coat, longer legs, and a more athletic build. A solitary, nocturnal hunter, it preys on rodents, small birds, reptiles, and fish. Highly adaptable, it thrives in forests, plantations, and farmland. It is also the wild ancestor of the Bengal cat domestic breed.
funFact: The leopard cat is the wild ancestor of the domestic Bengal cat, created by crossing leopard cats with domestic cats in the 1960s to produce a spotted pet with a wild appearance.

name: Jungle Cat
dangerNotes: Avoids humans. Will scratch and bite if cornered.
description: Despite its name, the jungle cat actually prefers open habitats such as wetlands, grasslands, and scrub rather than closed forest. It is the largest Felis species and has a plain tawny coat, long legs, a short tail with black tip, and characteristic tufted ears. An agile hunter of birds, rodents, and small reptiles, it was domesticated by ancient Egyptians and its mummified remains have been found in Egyptian tombs.
funFact: Ancient Egyptians domesticated the jungle cat alongside the African wildcat — mummified jungle cats have been found in Egyptian temples, suggesting they were kept as sacred animals.

name: Indo-Pacific Bottlenose Dolphin
dangerNotes: No significant threat to humans. Give space — approaching dolphins in boats can disrupt feeding and calf care.
description: The Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin is the dolphin most commonly seen in Thailand's coastal waters and around dive sites. Slightly smaller than the common bottlenose with a longer, more slender beak and spots on the belly in adults. Highly intelligent and social, it lives in fluid fission-fusion groups and is known to use marine sponges as foraging tools. A regular visitor to Thailand's gulf and Andaman Sea coasts.
funFact: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia have been observed wearing sea sponges on their beaks while foraging on the seafloor — a learned tool-use behaviour passed from mother to daughter.

name: Clouded Monitor
dangerNotes: Can deliver a powerful bite and whip painfully with its tail. Claws can lacerate. Saliva harbours bacteria. Non-venomous but avoid provocation.
description: The clouded monitor is a large, forest-dwelling relative of the water monitor, with fine pale spots and dashes on a dark background giving a clouded appearance. Found across Thailand's forests and woodland, it is an agile climber and powerful swimmer. A versatile predator, it hunts eggs, small mammals, birds, and carrion. Like all monitors, it has a forked tongue it uses to detect chemical signals from the environment.
funFact: Monitor lizards have forked tongues that work like stereo smell detectors — each tip samples the air separately and the brain measures the difference in chemical concentration to pinpoint the direction of prey.

name: Burmese Python
dangerNotes: One of the world's largest snakes — adults can exceed 5 metres and constrict with life-threatening force. Never approach alone. Give wide berth. Large adults can be extremely dangerous even without provocation.
description: The Burmese python is one of the five largest snake species on Earth, capable of exceeding 6 metres in exceptional individuals. A powerful constrictor, it kills prey by wrapping its body and squeezing until the prey's heart stops. It is semi-aquatic and an excellent swimmer, capable of remaining submerged for 30 minutes. In Thailand it is found in forests, wetlands, and near rivers. An invasive disaster in Florida, where it has devastated native wildlife.
funFact: The Burmese python can sense infrared radiation through heat-sensitive pits along its lips, allowing it to detect warm-blooded prey in complete darkness with pin-point accuracy.

name: Asian Elephant
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Elephants kill hundreds of people per year across Asia. Bulls in musth are especially unpredictable and lethal. Mothers with calves will charge without warning. Never approach, block an escape route, or get between a mother and her calf.
description: The Asian elephant is the largest land animal in Asia and one of the most intelligent creatures on Earth, with a complex social structure, long-term memory, and documented self-awareness. Smaller than the African elephant with distinctively smaller ears and a domed head, it lives in matriarchal family groups led by the oldest female. In Thailand it holds deep cultural and spiritual significance, serving historically as a war animal, working animal, and national symbol.
funFact: Asian elephants are one of the few animals that demonstrate self-awareness — individuals recognise themselves in mirrors, a cognitive ability shared only with great apes, dolphins, and a handful of other species.

name: Phayre's Langur
dangerNotes: Shy and arboreal. Poses no threat to humans.
description: Phayre's langur is a rare, forest-dependent leaf monkey found in northern and western Thailand. Recognisable by its distinctive white eye-rings and mouth patch set against a dark grey face, it lives in small groups in the high canopy. Severely threatened by deforestation, it is considered one of Asia's most endangered primates. Like all langurs, it has a specialised stomach to digest large amounts of leaves.
funFact: Phayre's langur has been the subject of long-term behavioural studies in Thailand — research showing that young males sometimes care for infants, unusual behaviour for Old World monkeys.

name: Slow Loris
dangerNotes: The only venomous primate. Produces a toxin by licking a gland on its arm and mixing it with saliva — bites can cause anaphylactic shock. Critically threatened by the illegal pet trade. Never handle.
description: The Sunda slow loris is the only venomous primate, producing toxic saliva by licking a specialised gland on its upper arm. Despite its wide-eyed, cuddly appearance, it is illegal to own and deeply unsuited to captivity. Nocturnal and arboreal, it moves slowly through the canopy feeding on tree gum, nectar, small animals, and fruit. Viral 'cute' videos have driven a devastating illegal pet trade that involves tooth-clipping and extreme animal suffering.
funFact: The slow loris is the only venomous primate on Earth. Its venom is created by mixing brachial gland secretions with saliva, and a bite can trigger anaphylactic shock in humans.

name: Binturong
dangerNotes: Generally placid but can bite powerfully if threatened. Wild individuals should not be approached.
description: The binturong, or bearcat, is a large, shaggy-furred viverrid with a prehensile tail — one of only two carnivores worldwide with a fully prehensile tail (the other being the kinkajou). It moves slowly through the high forest canopy, using all four limbs and its tail to navigate. Uniquely, its scent markings smell strongly of buttered popcorn due to the chemical 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. Primarily frugivorous, it is a critical disperser of strangler fig seeds.
funFact: A binturong's scent markings smell unmistakably like buttered popcorn — the same chemical responsible for popcorn's aroma (2-acetyl-1-pyrroline) is produced by its scent glands.

name: Banded Linsang
dangerNotes: Extremely secretive. Poses no threat to humans.
description: The banded linsang is one of the most elusive and least-known carnivores in Southeast Asia. Superficially resembling a civet but belonging to an entirely different family, it has a sinuous, cat-like body with a beautifully spotted and banded coat of cream and dark brown. A specialist of undisturbed primary forest, it hunts small vertebrates and insects high in the canopy. So rarely observed that almost nothing is known about its ecology in the wild.
funFact: The banded linsang is so elusive that virtually all knowledge of its behaviour comes from a handful of museum specimens and camera trap images — almost nothing is known of its ecology in the wild.

name: Spotted Linsang
dangerNotes: Extremely secretive. Poses no threat to humans.
description: The spotted linsang is the smaller of the two linsang species, found in the hill and montane forests of northern Thailand and the eastern Himalayas. With bold dark spots on a pale yellowish coat and a long banded tail, it is one of Asia's most visually striking small carnivores. Even rarer and less studied than the banded linsang, it is almost never seen in the wild and is known primarily from specimens.
funFact: The spotted linsang is considered one of the most primitive living members of the carnivore order — its skull retains features not seen in other living feliform carnivores.

name: Malay Weasel
dangerNotes: Secretive and avoids humans. Will bite if handled.
description: The Malay weasel is a rare and poorly-known mustelid endemic to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo. Unusual among weasels for its partially white or cream head contrasting with a pale brown-orange body. An active, fast-moving predator of small vertebrates and invertebrates, it is associated with undisturbed primary forest. Rarely photographed, it is primarily known from occasional camera trap captures and museum specimens.
funFact: The Malay weasel is so rarely seen that its basic ecological requirements — territory size, prey preferences, and breeding biology — are almost entirely unknown.

name: Sun Bear
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous if encountered. Unpredictable and capable of fatal mauling. The world's most aggressive bear — females with cubs are especially dangerous. Back away slowly. Never run.
description: The sun bear is the world's smallest bear and the most arboreal, equipped with enormous curved claws for climbing and an extraordinarily long tongue (up to 25 cm) for extracting honey and insects from tree hollows. Named for the distinctive yellow chest patch, it is also considered among the most aggressive bears — pound for pound, it can inflict devastating injuries. Found in rapidly declining numbers in Thailand's forests due to habitat loss and poaching.
funFact: The sun bear has the longest tongue relative to body size of any bear — up to 25 cm — used to lick out bee larvae, honey, and termites from deep inside logs and tree cavities.

name: Asian Black Bear
dangerNotes: Dangerous and unpredictable. Will charge and attack if surprised, cornered, or if cubs are nearby. Back away slowly without eye contact. Never run.
description: The Asian black bear, or moon bear, is a large bear with glossy black fur and a distinctive white or cream V-shaped chest patch. In Thailand it inhabits montane and mixed deciduous forests in the north. An accomplished climber, it spends considerable time in trees foraging for fruit, honey, and insects. Sadly, it is extensively targeted for bile farming in Asia — a practice condemned by conservationists worldwide. Encounters with humans in forest areas can be dangerous.
funFact: Asian black bears are capable climbers that build 'nests' in trees — bending branches into a platform — to feed on fruit and to sleep off the ground away from predators.

name: Gaur
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. The world's largest wild bovine — adult bulls can weigh over 1,000 kg. Cows with calves are highly aggressive. Give wide berth.
description: The gaur is the world's largest wild bovine, a massively built animal with a distinctive high dorsal ridge, sloping hindquarters, and grayish-white stockings on the lower legs. Adult bulls are among the most imposing land animals in Asia. Found in scattered forest populations across Thailand, they graze in clearings and forest edges. Despite their size, they are shy and tend to flee from humans — but cows with calves are extremely dangerous.
funFact: A bull gaur can weigh over 1,500 kg — heavier than a large domestic bull. Despite this mass, gaur can jump fences and move with surprising agility and speed when alarmed.

name: Fea's Muntjac
dangerNotes: Shy and elusive. Will flee from humans. No threat.
description: Fea's muntjac is a rare, dark-coated forest deer restricted to hilly and montane forests along the Thai-Myanmar border. Small and secretive, it is solitary and rarely observed. Males have short spiked antlers and elongated canine teeth. Like other muntjacs, it emits sharp, dog-like barks as an alarm call, earning muntjacs the nickname 'barking deer'. Very little is known about its ecology due to its extreme elusiveness.
funFact: Muntjacs are among the most evolutionarily ancient deer, with fossil records stretching back 15–35 million years. They have the lowest chromosome number of any mammal — some populations have just 6 chromosomes.

name: Dhole
dangerNotes: Pack-hunting predator capable of taking prey many times its size. Encounters in forest are rare but a cornered pack can be dangerous. Give wide berth.
description: The dhole, or Asian wild dog, is a highly social pack predator and one of Asia's most formidable hunters. Rusty-red with a black-tipped tail, it communicates through an extraordinary repertoire of whistles, screams, and clucks rather than howls. A pack of dholes can bring down animals as large as a gaur or sambar deer through coordinated pursuit and disembowelment. Severely endangered across its range due to habitat loss and prey depletion.
funFact: Dholes communicate using a unique whistle that no other wild canid makes — pack members use it to regroup after a hunt, and it can be heard from over a kilometre away in forest.

name: Fishing Cat
dangerNotes: Avoids humans. Capable of a powerful bite if cornered. No significant threat.
description: The fishing cat is a stocky, muscular wild cat uniquely adapted for aquatic life. With partially webbed forepaws, a short dense coat that repels water, and a short thick tail used as a rudder, it is a supremely capable swimmer and diver. It scoops or dives for fish and also catches frogs, molluscs, and water birds. Wetland destruction has made it one of Asia's more threatened cat species.
funFact: Fishing cats actually swim underwater to catch fish — they can submerge entirely and pursue prey below the surface, unlike most cats which merely scoop from the surface.

name: Asian Golden Cat
dangerNotes: A powerful medium-sized predator. Will avoid humans but is capable of serious injury if cornered.
description: The Asian golden cat is a medium-sized wild cat roughly twice the size of a domestic cat, with enormously variable coat colour — from golden-brown to dark grey to spotted morphs. A powerful, versatile predator, it hunts birds, reptiles, small deer, and livestock on occasion. Found in primary and secondary forest across Thailand, it is rarely observed in the wild and most of what is known comes from camera trap studies.
funFact: The Asian golden cat is sometimes called the 'fire cat' in local folklore — its pelt was believed to ward off tigers, and carrying a single hair was considered protective against tiger attack.

name: Marbled Cat
dangerNotes: Extremely secretive arboreal cat. No threat to humans.
description: The marbled cat is a small, exquisitely beautiful wild cat with a coat of swirling dark-edged blotches resembling polished marble on a tawny-brown ground. It has a disproportionately long, bushy tail nearly as long as its body — an adaptation for balance in the forest canopy where it spends most of its life hunting birds and squirrels. One of the least-studied wild cats in Asia due to its extreme rarity and arboreal, nocturnal habits.
funFact: The marbled cat has the longest tail relative to body length of any cat in Asia — almost as long as its body — used as a counterbalance for leaping between branches in the forest canopy.

name: White-handed Gibbon
dangerNotes: Shy and arboreal. Wild individuals avoid humans. Males can be territorial but pose little real threat.
description: The white-handed gibbon is Thailand's most widespread gibbon, a master of brachiation — swinging through the forest canopy using its impossibly long arms at speeds of up to 55 km/h. Pairs are monogamous and bond through elaborate, loud duet songs that echo through the forest at dawn. Coat colour varies from black to cream and is not sex-linked. Severely threatened by deforestation and the illegal pet trade.
funFact: A gibbon's morning song can be heard up to 2 kilometres through the forest — mated pairs sing elaborate, coordinated duets that reinforce their bond and advertise territory simultaneously.

name: Pileated Gibbon
dangerNotes: Arboreal and avoids humans. No significant threat.
description: The pileated gibbon is found primarily in eastern Thailand and shows dramatic sexual dichromatism — males are black with white hands and feet and a white brow cap; females are cream with a black face and chest patch. Like all gibbons, pairs bond for life and fill the forest with loud, complex dawn songs. Restricted to a relatively small range in Thailand, it is threatened by deforestation and wildlife trade.
funFact: Male and female pileated gibbons look so different in colour that early naturalists classified them as separate species — males are black, females are cream or buff.

name: Agile Gibbon
dangerNotes: Shy and arboreal. No threat to humans.
description: The agile gibbon is found in the forests of southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula, living in monogamous pairs in the high forest canopy. Males are typically black with white eyebrows and cheeks; females are buff or golden-brown. It is a specialist frugivore, supplementing its diet with leaves, flowers, and insects. One of the fastest brachiating animals, it can swing between branches at remarkable speed and agility.
funFact: Gibbons are the fastest and most agile of all tree-dwelling mammals — they can brachiate at up to 55 km/h and cover up to 15 metres in a single swing.

name: Irrawaddy Dolphin
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The Irrawaddy dolphin is a unique, blunt-headed dolphin with no distinct beak and a highly flexible neck, giving it an unusually expressive face. Found in coastal and riverine waters across Southeast Asia, it is famous for its cooperative behaviour with fishermen — actively herding fish toward nets in exchange for fish scraps. Some populations, such as those in the Mekong River, are critically small and face imminent extinction.
funFact: Irrawaddy dolphins in Myanmar have a centuries-old tradition of cooperative fishing with humans — they herd fish toward nets on signal and are rewarded with a share of the catch.

name: Dumeril's Monitor
dangerNotes: Large and powerful. Can bite, scratch, and whip with tail. Give distance.
description: Dumeril's monitor is a large, semi-aquatic monitor lizard with a distinctive orange or reddish head in adults, contrasting with a dark, banded body. Found in lowland rainforest and mangrove systems of southern Thailand, it is a powerful predator that feeds heavily on crabs, fish, and frogs. Juveniles have vivid orange-red heads that fade as the animal matures. Heavily exploited for skin and meat.
funFact: Juvenile Dumeril's monitors have brilliant orange-red heads thought to mimic venomous centipedes or millipedes — a form of Batesian mimicry to deter predators.

name: Roughneck Monitor
dangerNotes: Large arboreal monitor. Can bite and scratch defensively. Avoid handling.
description: The roughneck monitor is a specialist arboreal monitor named for the strongly keeled scales on its neck and back. With a slender black body and small yellow spots, it is supremely adapted to life high in the forest canopy, rarely descending to the ground. It hunts bird eggs, small vertebrates, and invertebrates in the high canopy of primary rainforest. Extremely sensitive to habitat disturbance and found only in intact primary forest.
funFact: The roughneck monitor is so specialised for arboreal life that its hind limbs have evolved a near-opposite orientation to ground monitors, allowing it to grip vertical branches more effectively.

name: Blood Python
dangerNotes: Heavy-bodied constrictor with a notoriously defensive temperament. Will bite readily and can inflict serious lacerations. Adults can constrict a human limb. Do not handle.
description: The blood python is a short, massively heavy-bodied python with a striking pattern of deep red, orange, and brown blotches on a tan or yellowish background — the vivid colouring responsible for its common name. Found in the lowland swamps and peat forests of southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula, it is a sedentary ambush predator of small mammals. Despite a reputation for aggression, it is extensively hunted for the leather trade.
funFact: Blood pythons have one of the highest weight-to-length ratios of any python — a 1.5-metre individual can weigh over 20 kg, making them one of the most massive short pythons in the world.

name: King Cobra
dangerNotes: The world's longest venomous snake and one of the most dangerous. A single bite can deliver enough neurotoxic venom to kill an elephant. Death can occur within 30 minutes. Immediately leave the area. Seek emergency medical care at once.
description: The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake, reaching over 5 metres in exceptional individuals. Despite its size, it is a specialist predator of other snakes, including other cobras. When threatened it rears up to one-third of its body height, spreads a broad hood, and growls — one of the few snakes with an audible vocalisation. Females are devoted mothers, guarding their nest for weeks until hatching. An apex predator revered and feared across Asia.
funFact: The king cobra is the only snake that builds a nest — the female pushes leaf litter into a mound, lays her eggs inside, then guards them ferociously for the entire 60–90 day incubation period.

name: Saltwater Crocodile
dangerNotes: The world's largest living reptile and apex predator. Responsible for hundreds of human fatalities annually across Asia. Do not approach water's edge in known habitat. They can lunge at tremendous speed onto land. Treat any sighting as an immediate danger.
description: The saltwater crocodile is the world's largest living reptile, with large males exceeding 6 metres and 1,000 kg. An apex ambush predator, it can remain submerged with only eyes and nostrils above the waterline for hours before lunging at prey with explosive speed. It is capable of taking prey as large as water buffalo and has been responsible for fatal attacks on humans. Despite a fearsome reputation, it is also one of conservation's great success stories, recovering from near-extinction after legal protection.
funFact: The saltwater crocodile has the most powerful bite force ever measured in a living animal — over 16,000 newtons — more than twice the bite force of the next-strongest animal.

name: Indochinese Box Turtle
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The Indochinese box turtle is a small, beautifully patterned turtle with a high-domed shell of olive, brown, and black. Uniquely, it has a hinged plastron (lower shell) that closes completely when the turtle withdraws — providing near-total protection from predators. Critically endangered due to mass collection for Asian food and medicine markets. Wild populations have been devastated and it is considered functionally extinct across much of its range.
funFact: Box turtles can completely seal themselves inside their shell by closing a hinged lower shell — making the animal virtually impossible for most predators to penetrate.

name: Impressed Tortoise
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The impressed tortoise is a medium-sized highland tortoise with a distinctive flat-topped, deeply sculptured shell that gives it its name. Found in the cool, humid montane forests of northern Thailand and neighbouring countries, it is associated with bamboo forest. Unlike many tortoises, it prefers cooler temperatures and is sensitive to heat. Threatened by collection for food and traditional medicine, and by habitat loss.
funFact: The impressed tortoise is the only tortoise in the world known to actively construct a nest — it pushes leaves into a pile, buries its eggs inside, and may briefly guard the mound.

name: Asian Brown Tortoise
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. May hiss if disturbed.
description: The Asian brown tortoise is the largest tortoise in mainland Asia and the fourth largest in the world, with a massive, heavy-domed dark brown shell and sturdy elephant-like legs. It inhabits humid tropical and montane forests and is closely tied to water sources. A remarkable nesting behaviour sets it apart from all other tortoises: the female pushes leaf litter into a large nest mound and actively guards it for weeks after laying.
funFact: The Asian brown tortoise is the only tortoise species known to actively guard its nest — the female will aggressively charge and bite perceived threats to her nest mound for up to several weeks.

name: Green Sea Turtle
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Do not touch, ride, or disturb — feeding turtles are protected.
description: The green sea turtle is the largest hard-shelled sea turtle and one of the most iconic marine animals. Named not for its shell colour but for the greenish fat beneath its skin — a result of its herbivorous diet of seagrass and algae. An extraordinary navigator, it migrates thousands of kilometres between feeding grounds and the beach where it was born to nest. Both nesting females and feeding individuals are protected in Thai waters.
funFact: Green sea turtles navigate back to the exact beach where they were born to lay their own eggs — using Earth's magnetic field as a GPS system to find the precise location decades later.

name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Critically endangered — never disturb or touch.
description: The hawksbill sea turtle is one of the world's most critically endangered sea turtles, prized for generations for its beautifully patterned shell — 'tortoiseshell' — driving it to the brink of extinction. Its narrow, pointed beak allows it to reach into coral crevices to feed on sponges, which form the bulk of its diet. A keystone species of coral reef ecosystems, it helps control sponge populations that would otherwise overgrow coral. Seen occasionally at Thailand's reefs.
funFact: Hawksbill turtles are among the very few animals that can eat toxic sponges without ill effects — and by doing so, they prevent sponges from smothering coral reefs.

name: Olive Ridley Sea Turtle
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Protected species — do not disturb.
description: The olive ridley is the smallest and most abundant sea turtle, named for its pale olive-grey heart-shaped shell. It is famous for its arribada behaviour — mass synchronised nesting events where thousands of females come ashore to nest on the same beach simultaneously over a few days. A highly migratory species, it traverses vast ocean distances between feeding and nesting sites. Occasionally seen in Thailand's Andaman Sea coastal waters.
funFact: Olive ridley turtles perform one of nature's great mass spectacles — the 'arribada', where up to 500,000 females emerge to nest on a single beach in just a few days, filling every metre of sand.

name: Indochinese Tiger
dangerNotes: An apex predator and man-eater in extremely rare circumstances. If encountered in the wild: do not run, do not turn your back, back away slowly while facing the animal. A tiger encounter in Thailand is exceptionally rare and an extraordinary privilege.
description: The Indochinese tiger is one of the rarest animals on Earth, with only an estimated 160–230 individuals remaining in the wild, the majority in Thailand's Western Forest Complex. Smaller and darker than the Bengal tiger, it is a supreme predator of large ungulates such as sambar, gaur, and wild pig. Thailand's conservation efforts — particularly at Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary — represent one of the tiger's last genuine strongholds in Southeast Asia.
funFact: Thailand is one of the very few places where tiger numbers are actually increasing — rigorous law enforcement and prey management in the Western Forest Complex has allowed a slow but genuine recovery.

name: Clouded Leopard
dangerNotes: A powerful ambush predator with the largest canine teeth relative to skull size of any living cat. Wild encounters are extraordinarily rare. Keep distance if encountered.
description: The clouded leopard is one of Asia's most secretive and beautiful cats, with a coat of irregularly edged dark-margined blotches resembling the dappled light of a forest canopy. It has the longest canine teeth relative to skull size of any living felid — proportionally similar to the extinct sabre-toothed cats. A supreme arboreal predator, it can hang upside down from branches using its large paws and exceptionally flexible ankles. Almost nothing is known of its behaviour in the wild.
