funFact: The clouded leopard can rotate its hind ankles backward — allowing it to descend trees head-first like a squirrel, a unique ability among large cats.

name: Flat-headed Cat
dangerNotes: Extremely shy and reclusive. No threat to humans. Sightings are extraordinarily rare.
description: The flat-headed cat is one of the world's rarest and least-known wild cats, so elusive that few field biologists have ever seen one alive. Its flattened skull, small rounded ears, and partially webbed feet are adaptations for a highly aquatic lifestyle fishing in streams and rivers. Its eyes are positioned to give binocular vision when looking downward into water. Critically threatened by river pollution and deforestation, it may be one of Southeast Asia's most endangered mammals.
funFact: The flat-headed cat's teeth are proportionally larger and sharper than any other small cat, angled backwards to grip slippery fish — essentially it has evolved the dental structure of a fishing trap.

name: Malayan Tapir
dangerNotes: Generally placid but can be unpredictable and surprisingly fast. Mothers with young are defensive. A tapir bite can cause serious injury. Maintain distance.
description: The Malayan tapir is the largest tapir species and the only one native to Asia, instantly recognisable by its dramatic two-tone black-and-white colouring — a 'saddle' of white across the back and hindquarters against a black body. This disruptive colouration breaks up the animal's outline in dappled moonlight. A prehistoric-looking animal, tapirs are most closely related to horses and rhinos. An excellent swimmer, it readily enters water to bathe, cool off, and escape predators.
funFact: A tapir's short, flexible prehensile trunk — an extension of the nose and upper lip — is used to sniff the air, grasp leaves, and even as a snorkel when crossing deep rivers.

name: Sumatran Rhinoceros
dangerNotes: Functionally extinct in Thailand and virtually extinct globally — fewer than 80 remain. Encounters are essentially impossible. Historically could be extremely dangerous if surprised.
description: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the smallest and hairiest of the living rhino species, and the closest living relative of the extinct woolly rhinoceros. Once widespread across Southeast Asia, it is now critically endangered with fewer than 80 individuals surviving, mostly in small populations in Sumatra. Thailand's population has been considered functionally extinct for decades. It is a solitary, forest-dependent browser with two horns. Its survival is considered extremely precarious.
funFact: The Sumatran rhino is the only surviving two-horned rhino in Asia and the closest living relative of the woolly mammoth's era rhinos — it even has a reddish-brown coat of coarse hair.

name: Eld's Deer
dangerNotes: Shy and will flee. Rutting males with antlers should be given distance.
description: Eld's deer, or the brow-antlered deer, is an elegant, medium-sized deer with distinctive antlers in which the brow tine and main beam form a continuous sweeping curve rather than a sharp fork — giving it an unusually graceful silhouette. Found in open grassland and swampy forest, it was once widespread across Southeast Asia but is now restricted to tiny fragmented populations in Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, and India's Manipur state.
funFact: Eld's deer was named after Lt. Percy Eld, a 19th-century US Navy officer — but the deer had been sacred to the Meitei people of Manipur, who called it Sangai, for centuries before its scientific description.

name: Sunda Pangolin
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Will roll into a ball if threatened. The world's most trafficked mammal — if you see one, report it to wildlife authorities.
description: The Sunda pangolin is a unique, scale-covered insectivore and the world's most heavily trafficked wild mammal — an estimated one million have been taken from the wild in the past decade for their scales and meat in Asian black markets. Related to no other living animal, it is covered in overlapping keratin scales and rolls into a tight ball when threatened. A nocturnal specialist, it locates ant and termite colonies using an extraordinary sense of smell and excavates them with powerful claws.
funFact: A pangolin's tongue is longer than its entire body — up to 40 cm — coiled up in its chest when not in use, and can flick in and out 160 times per minute to lap up insects.

name: Chinese Pangolin
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Rolls into a ball if threatened. If encountered, report to wildlife authorities immediately — this species is critically endangered.
description: The Chinese pangolin is the most northerly-ranging pangolin species, found in hilly and montane forests of northern Thailand and southern China. Like the Sunda pangolin, it is critically endangered due to poaching — its scales are falsely believed to have medicinal properties. Distinguished from the Sunda pangolin by larger scales, a bare underside to the tail tip, and the presence of external ears. Both pangolin species in Thailand face existential threat from illegal wildlife trade.
funFact: Pangolin scales are made of the same material as human fingernails — keratin — and have zero proven medicinal properties, yet demand for them has made pangolins the most trafficked mammal on Earth.

name: Dugong
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Extremely gentle. Do not chase or approach — they are shy and easily stressed.
description: The dugong is the only strictly marine mammal that feeds exclusively on seagrass. A gentle, slow-moving relative of the manatee, it uses its muscular, bristled snout to uproot seagrass from the seafloor. Thailand's last significant dugong population grazes in the seagrass meadows off Trang province. Dugongs are believed to have inspired mermaid legends — sailors mistook their silhouettes for human figures surfacing to breathe.
funFact: Dugongs are believed to have inspired mermaid legends worldwide — their silhouette when surfacing, combined with their human-like eyes and the way they cradle calves, sparked centuries of sailor mythology.

name: Siamese Crocodile
dangerNotes: A large, powerful predator capable of fatal attack. Wild individuals are extremely rare — any encounter is extraordinary. Do not approach water edges in known habitat.
description: The Siamese crocodile is one of the world's most critically endangered reptiles, now functionally extinct across most of its former range due to hunting and habitat loss. A medium-sized freshwater crocodile, it was once widespread across Southeast Asia's rivers and lakes. The few surviving wild individuals are mostly confined to remote areas of Cambodia and Laos, with occasional records in Thailand. Most 'wild' crocodiles in Thailand are farm escapees — true wild Siamese crocodiles are extraordinarily rare.
funFact: The Siamese crocodile was once thought to be extinct in the wild entirely — but in 2000, a small wild population was rediscovered in Cambodia's Cardamom Mountains, sparking intensive conservation efforts.

name: Asian Giant Softshell Turtle
dangerNotes: The world's largest freshwater turtle. Powerful jaws can deliver a severe bite. Do not approach if encountered.
description: Cantor's giant softshell turtle is the world's largest freshwater turtle, with a shell over 2 metres in large adults. It is almost entirely aquatic, spending 95% of its time buried and motionless in sandy riverbeds with only its eyes and nostrils above the sediment, ambushing crabs, fish, and molluscs. It surfaces only briefly twice per day to breathe. Rarely seen and deeply endangered by hunting, sand mining, and river development.
funFact: Cantor's giant softshell turtle spends 95% of its life buried in river sand, surfacing to breathe for just two brief moments each day — making it one of the hardest large animals in the world to observe.

name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Critically important nesting species — never disturb nesting females or hatchlings.
description: The leatherback is the world's largest living turtle and one of the largest reptiles, with some individuals exceeding 900 kg. Unlike other sea turtles, it has no hard shell — instead, its back is covered in a mosaic of tiny bone fragments embedded in tough, leathery skin. A specialist on jellyfish, it can dive deeper than 1,200 metres and maintain a body temperature well above the surrounding ocean. Nesting females once visited Thailand's Andaman coast in significant numbers.
funFact: The leatherback sea turtle can maintain a body temperature up to 18°C warmer than the surrounding ocean water — a form of near-thermoregulation unique among living reptiles.
nativeRegions: Ranging into Arctic and sub-Antarctic waters
